22455:
• Every classroom must be equipped with a sensor that continuously measures carbon dioxide in the air, within 6 months.
  • Maximum limit set at 1000 ppm of CO2, lowered to 800 ppm during a declared pandemic period.
  • The department must publish the sensor data on its website every week.
  • An action protocol must be applied by schools when the CO2 standard is exceeded.
  • Every classroom must have an air exchanger or purifier, supplied and paid for by the department, within 12 months.
  • Exchangers and purifiers must be inspected at least every six months, with reports made public.
  • The department must ensure annual follow-up on corrective measures taken as a result of inspections.
22465:
• Requires the government to set by regulation a maximum number of patients per nurse, licensed practical nurse and orderly
  • Applies to emergency departments, surgery, general and specialized medicine, as well as long-term care centres (CHSLDs)
  • Creates a 7-member advisory committee to recommend these ratios to the government
  • The committee includes representatives from unions, professional orders and institution management
  • The committee must submit a report on the impact of the regulation, first in 2023 and then every 5 years
  • This report must be tabled in the National Assembly and studied by a committee
  • The government has one year after the Act is assented to in order to adopt the regulation on ratios
22471:
• Adds to the preamble of the Charter the importance of preserving a healthy environment for human health.
  • Recognizes the right of every person to live in a healthy environment that respects biodiversity.
  • Elevates this right to the status of a fundamental right, like the other rights in the Charter.
  • Removes the restriction limiting this right to the measures and standards provided for by law.
  • This change could facilitate legal recourse based on this environmental right.
22581:
• Amends the Act respecting educational childcare services to guarantee the right to these services.
  • Removes two paragraphs from section 2 of the Act, which limited the scope of this right.
  • The Act would come into force five years after its assent.
22597:
• Makes special educational projects and concentration programs free of charge in public schools, up to $5,000 per year.
  • Includes in the free-of-charge provision selection fees, file-opening fees, test administration fees, and staff training fees.
  • Prohibits school service centres from establishing a special project school in more than one building.
  • Except in special cases: several buildings are permitted only if they are located no more than 250 metres from one another.
22599:
• Amends the Act respecting the Generations Fund, intended to reduce Québec's public debt.
  • Sets a capitalization threshold of $100 billion for this fund.
  • Requires that the allocation and amounts of the Fund remain unchanged until this threshold is reached.
  • Exceptions remain possible only where the Act itself provides for them.
  • The Act would come into force on the date of its official assent.
22639:
• The Minister of Finance will have to ensure gender equality and diversity are considered in budgetary decisions.
  • A report on gender- and diversity-based impacts must be tabled after each budget.
  • This report must also be tabled after an economic update announcing new measures.
  • The competent parliamentary committee must study these tabled reports.
  • The Minister of Finance will publish an annual analysis of the gender- and diversity-based impacts of fiscal measures.
  • The President of the Treasury Board will also publish a similar annual analysis of government spending.

22765:
• Requires the school to provide equivalent educational services if it cannot provide the services required by law.

  • Requires the authorization of the parent or guardian for a minor student.

22767:

22797:
• Requires elementary schools, secondary schools and adult education centres to adopt a policy against sexual violence within one year.
  • The policy must include mandatory training, security measures, a complaint process and psychosocial support services.
  • Imposes a code of conduct to govern relationships between staff and students, including students of full age.
  • Sets maximum time limits: 7 days to intervene, 90 days to process a complaint or report.
  • Requires the formation of a committee including management, staff, students and parents to develop and review the policy.
  • Provides for annual accountability reporting on complaints, training and sanctions applied.

22799:
• The Caisse de dépôt should ensure that its investments have sustainable social and environmental impacts.
  • Its mission now explicitly includes the sustainable economic development of Québec.
  • The annual report submitted to the Minister of Finance must detail the social and environmental impacts of investments.
  • This report must be tabled in the National Assembly before April 15 each year.
  • The government may set out by regulation the criteria for assessing these impacts.
  • A regulation may also specify how these impacts must be publicly disclosed.
22831:
• The Minister will be required to take temporary residents into account in multi-year immigration planning.
  • The multi-year policy directions will target the number of persons admitted on a temporary or permanent basis.
  • The annual plan will have to specify the expected number of temporary residents, in addition to permanent immigrants.
  • The number of selection decisions provided for in the annual plan will also cover temporary stays.
22899:
• Renders invalid lease clauses that prohibit pets.
  • Applies to leases already in effect, not only to new leases.
  • The government must remove prohibition mentions from mandatory lease forms within 30 days.
  • The definition of "pet" is based on the Animal Welfare and Safety Act.
  • Other existing tenant protections in the Civil Code remain unchanged.
23167:
• Adds an official emblematic insect for Québec, the white admiral (Limenitis arthemis arthemis).
  • Amends the Act respecting the flag and emblems of Québec to include this new symbol.
  • Comes into force upon assent of the Act.
23285:
• Requires authorization from the Minister of the Environment before adding a project to the Québec infrastructure plan.
  • The Minister must refuse a project that jeopardizes the achievement of Québec's greenhouse gas reduction targets.
  • The government will set out by regulation the criteria for analyzing climate impacts, with the assistance of environmental experts.
  • The Minister may impose conditions or restrictions to reduce emissions related to a project.
  • The Minister may amend or add conditions to a project that has already been authorized, if necessary.
  • The Québec infrastructure plan will have to include a report on the emissions and climate impact of projects.
  • Public bodies will be required to provide the Minister with the information necessary for this climate assessment.
23425:
• Prohibits evicting a tenant for the purpose of converting their dwelling into short-term tourist accommodation.
  • Amends section 1959 of the Civil Code of Québec to add this exception.
  • Aims to protect tenants against the conversion of residential dwellings into tourist rentals.
  • The act would come into force on the date of its assent.
23753:
• Requires CEGEPs, universities and other educational institutions to adopt a study-family-work balance policy.
  • Policy intended for student parents or caregivers, to be adopted within 6 months and implemented within 12 months.
  • Creates special statuses: student parent, caregiver, deemed enrolled or enrolled full-time.
  • Provides for leaves, exam accommodations and measures facilitating access to childcare services.
  • Requires a joint committee consulting affected persons to develop and review the policy.
  • Requires institutions to report annually to the minister on the implementation of their policy.
  • Allows the minister to impose oversight measures or have obligations carried out at the institution's expense in cases of non-compliance.
23955:
• Creates a citizen initiative right requiring the BAPE to hold a hearing if a petition reaches certain thresholds.
  • Requires 40,000 signatures (including 5,000 per region, in 3 regions) for a national issue, or 15,000 for a regional issue.
  • The chair and vice-chair of the BAPE will be appointed by the National Assembly, following an in-camera interview with MNAs.
  • Allows the BAPE to require a report on a project's greenhouse gas emissions and its reduction measures.
  • The government will have to publicly justify authorizing a project despite a refusal recommended by the BAPE.
  • Abolishes the Comité consultatif sur les évaluations environnementales stratégiques, whose tasks are transferred to the BAPE.
  • Gives the BAPE the power to recommend that a project be subject to a full environmental assessment.

24137:
• Amends the Act to Foster the Economic and Social Inclusion of Persons and Families to Overcome Poverty for recipients of the Social Solidarity Program.
  • Allows these recipients to earn employment income without a reduction in their benefit.
  • Aligns the amount of permitted employment income with that of the Basic Income Program.
  • The Act would come into force on the date of its official assent.
24211:
• Creates the position of Parliamentary Budget Officer, appointed by the National Assembly for a non-renewable seven-year term.
  • This officer provides non-partisan analysis of Québec's public finances, budget forecasts and economic trends.
  • The officer must produce an annual report on economic outlooks, a portrait of public finances twice a year, and a report on intergenerational equity every three years.
  • Transfers responsibility for certifying the pre-election report on public finances from the Auditor General to this new officer.
  • Members of the National Assembly may request a confidential assessment of the cost of a proposed expenditure or measure.
  • Departments and public bodies must provide the officer with requested documents and information, notwithstanding access to information legislation.
  • The officer and staff benefit from judicial immunities and are bound to secrecy regarding confidential data.

24223:
• Prohibits driving with a blood alcohol level of 50 mg to 80 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood.
  • Immediate licence suspension upon a first offence within this new blood alcohol range.
  • 3-day suspension for a first offence, 7 days for a second offence within 5 years.
  • Suspension of at least 90 days for a third or subsequent offence within 5 years.
  • Licence recovery conditional on an assessment of the person's relationship with alcohol or drugs.
  • Possible requirement to complete an alcohol or drug awareness program.
  • Possibility of requiring the installation of an ignition interlock device in certain cases.
24279:
• Grants each Member the right to visit certain administrative institutions (departments, municipalities, schools, hospitals, etc.).
  • Allows the Member to speak confidentially with any person on site, except ministers.
  • Authorizes the Member to be accompanied by an employee, an expert, and a journalist during the visit.
  • Limits visits to once every three months per institution, for a maximum of two consecutive days.
  • Requires written notice of at least 10 business days before the visit.
  • Allows the institution to refuse or restrict the visit only for serious security reasons.
  • Provides for recourse to the Superior Court if a refusal is deemed unjustified.
24453:
• Aims to reduce food waste by half by 2030 through a national strategy.
  • Requires businesses and manufacturers to offer their unsold goods to organizations before discarding them.
  • Creates a public registry of unsold goods quantities and donation agreements reached.
  • Prohibits deliberately rendering unsold food or goods unfit for consumption.
  • Creates a Repair Fund to encourage the repair of goods and the circular economy.
  • Prevents manufacturers from refusing a warranty if the good was repaired by a third party.
  • Provides for fines of up to $250,000 (individuals) or $1.5 million (businesses).

• Specifies the order of flags: the fleurdelisé on the left, or in the centre if three flags are displayed.
  • Requires a public ceremony for Flag Day in every RCM or isolated local municipality.
  • Allows the minister to appoint inspectors to verify compliance with the Act.
  • Requires the Québec flag on federal buildings, national parks and municipal parks in Québec.
  • Requires the flag on the building housing the riding office of provincial and federal members.
  • Sets out the rules for disposing of a worn flag (dignified burning or cutting into strips).
  • Requires members to provide a Québec flag free of charge to anyone who requests one.

• Extends the right to install surveillance mechanisms to users of rehabilitation centres, not just CHSLDs.
  • Targets 4 types of centres: intellectual disability, physical disability, dependency, youth in difficulty.
  • For a user under 14 years of age, the camera must be installed by their representative.
  • Consent to surveillance of a user under 14 years of age must come from their representative.
  • The institutions concerned will have to inform new users of this right upon admission.
  • Adjusts posting and information obligations to include the rehabilitation centres concerned.
  • The Act comes into force upon its official assent.
24727:
• Adds a new section 45.1 to Québec's Charter of human rights and freedoms.
  • Enshrines the right of every person to decent housing.
  • This right includes security of tenure, availability, accessibility and affordability of housing.
  • Draws on international instruments recognizing the right to housing (UN, OAS).
  • The Act comes into force on the date of its assent.
25171:
• Sets the objective of achieving carbon neutrality in Québec by 2050.
  • Requires the government to take the necessary measures to reduce GHG emissions.
  • Imposes a reduction target of at least 37.5% compared to 1990, increasing with each period.
  • Requires a review of the targets every five years.
  • Allows the government to set different targets depending on the sector of activity.
  • Provides for public consultation in a parliamentary committee before setting or revising a target.
  • Requires a public opinion from the advisory committee on climate change before any parliamentary consultation.
25237:
• The bill creates a national digital identity, managed by the Minister of Cybersecurity and Digital Technology, to securely access government services online.
  • It gives the minister new powers over telecommunications, cybersecurity and the government's information technology.
Part 1 Act respecting the Ministère de la Cybersécurité et du Numérique
  • The minister manages the national digital identity and provides digital credentials to citizens.
  • The minister becomes the official source of the government's digital data and creates a registry to keep it.
  • The minister must propose to the government an overall plan for telecommunications networks useful to the state.
  • The minister may create and manage their own connectivity network, with no commercial purpose.
  • The minister no longer needs Treasury Board approval to lease buildings related to telecommunications.
  • The minister may offer public bodies specialized technology goods and services, in addition to cloud services.
Part 2 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale
  • The Minister of Cybersecurity collaborates on setting up a government multi-service portal.
Part 3 Act respecting the governance and management of information resources
  • Public bodies must use the minister's services for their cybersecurity activities.
  • A public body must notify the minister in the event of a serious breach of its data security.
  • The government may extend this notification requirement to any person or business managing essential infrastructure.
  • Public bodies must collect official data from the source designated by the minister, unless the government grants an exception.
  • The chief information officer may delegate their powers to other people.
Part 4 Act respecting the legal framework for information technology
  • The harmonization committee, which advised on information technology, is removed.
  • It is now the minister, not the Treasury Board, who approves businesses offering digital certification services.
Part 5 Tax Administration Act, Health Insurance Act, Regulation respecting land registration and other regulations
  • Technical adjustments to align with the new rules on digital identity.

Who voted for, against or abstained

No list of names exists for this law. It was passed by voice: the Speaker asks “Is this motion carried?” and members answer from their seats. If no one objects, it passes unanimously. If a party answers “On division”, it passes by a majority, without anyone being counted.

A list of names exists only when a party asks for a recorded division: each member then stands for, against or abstaining, and their name is written down. How it was passed, on the Assembly’s website.
25291:
• Creates a special parliamentary committee of 5 members to study the documents from the Grenier inquiry on Option Canada.
  • The committee identifies which documents must remain confidential, with unanimous consent required.
  • Documents not deemed confidential are made public in the committee's final report.
  • The committee may retain a special adviser to make recommendations on the confidential nature of documents.
  • The Chief Electoral Officer must transmit the documents within 30 days of assent.
  • Documents deemed confidential will automatically become public after 25 years.
  • No civil action may arise from facts revealed as a result of this Act.
25363:
• Recognizes the right of older persons to remain at home for as long as possible, with appropriate support.
  • Guarantees rights: affordable and adapted housing, protection against abuse, dignified end of life, financial security.
  • Establishes a national strategy for the autonomy and home care of older persons.
  • Requires the government to adopt a five-year action plan with concrete targets for care and housing.
  • Provides for a first action plan to be published within six months of the Act's passage.
  • Assigns the Commission des droits de la personne to ensure respect for these new rights.
  • Provides for tax measures, rent regulation, and financial support for low-income seniors.
25393:
• Makes all women or pregnant persons in Québec eligible for health insurance and prescription drug coverage, regardless of their migratory status.
  • Eliminates the usual waiting period under health insurance for women or pregnant persons.
  • Grants eligibility if the person intends to remain in Québec for more than 6 months, including 2 months after childbirth.
  • Maintains coverage for 2 years after the expected date of childbirth for persons not otherwise eligible.
  • Provides for 12 weeks of eligibility following a pregnancy termination.
  • Requires a medical certificate confirming the pregnancy and expected date of childbirth for registration.
  • Provides that the Act comes into force on the date of its assent, with transitional rules for ongoing cases.

• Allows municipalities to claim compensation from the government for land transferred to a school service centre.
  • The compensation corresponds to the value of the land as entered on the property assessment roll.
  • Extends from 45 to 60 days the time limit for municipalities to give their opinion on school planning.
  • Requires school service centres to prioritize optimal density of land use.
  • Gives the minister the power to cancel the obligation to transfer land if densification is not prioritized.
  • Reduces existing compensation by the amount of any compensation already received for the same land.
25631:
• Creates a common school network bringing together public schools and "contracted" private schools that choose to join it.
  • Prohibits any selection of students upon entry into schools within this common network.
  • Gradually cuts public funding for private schools that refuse to join the common network.
  • Requires free tuition and equal funding for all schools in the network, including special educational projects.
  • Establishes catchment-area school maps, with one designated school per address, reviewed annually.
  • Provides for compensation measures to reduce socio-economic inequalities between school catchment areas.
  • Requires contracted schools to maintain financial transparency, undergo external audits, and be subject to oversight by the minister.

25709:
• The SAAQ will have to send a notice of payment 30 days before the deadline for vehicle registration.
  • A similar notice will also have to be sent 30 days before the driver's licence renewal deadline.
  • These notices must comply with the form and content determined by the SAAQ.
  • An owner or licence holder cannot be found guilty of driving without a valid right if the SAAQ did not send the required notice.
  • The Act comes into force upon its official assent.
25793:
• This bill strengthens the state's secularism in Québec's public and private schools.
  • It adds rules on uncovered faces, religious symbols, and the quality of teaching.
Part 1 Education Act
  • Specifies that public school is based on state secularism and equality between men and women.
  • Students must have their faces uncovered in schools and training centres.
  • Children schooled at home and their parents must also have their faces uncovered in front of the school service centre.
  • Anyone providing services to students or in contact with them must have their face uncovered.
  • Students must respect equality between the sexes and avoid any bullying related to racism, sexual orientation, a disability, or another characteristic.
  • Schools and training centres must adopt codes of conduct including these obligations.
  • Bans the wearing of religious symbols by more school service centre staff members and by certain people under a service contract.
  • Employees already working or under contract before the bill was tabled are not covered by this ban.
  • Sets rules for school employees' requests for leave on religious grounds, especially when they affect mandatory school attendance.
  • Decisions by members of governing boards and school service centres must be free of any religious considerations.
  • Statements and decisions by school service centre staff must respect state secularism.
  • School service centres must adopt a code of ethics for governing board members.
  • Bans the use of school and centre premises for religious practices.
  • Bans anyone from using a religious belief to influence a decision provided for by the Act.
  • Teachers must submit a teaching plan to the principal, who must evaluate them each year.
  • Creates a committee on the quality of educational services to help school administrations.
  • The education minister can set an exam schedule and order a school service centre to comply with a law or rule.
  • Certain decisions by the minister, such as suspending a teaching licence, apply even if the teacher challenges them before the Administrative Tribunal of Québec.
  • Expands the requirement to use only French in communications with students and between employees of French-language centres.
  • Some rules apply even if they conflict with certain rights under the rights charters.
Part 2 Act on Private Education
  • Imposes the same rules on uncovered faces, religious symbols, and codes of conduct on private institutions.
  • Private schools not recognized for subsidies must also follow the uncovered face rule for their staff.
  • Some rules apply even if they conflict with certain rights under the rights charters.
Part 3 Regulation respecting ethics and professional conduct standards
  • Makes matching adjustments for board members of a French-language school service centre.

26021:
• This bill amends 11 laws and regulations affecting the world of work in Québec.
  • It mainly changes rules on workplace accidents, unions, labour standards, and occupational health and safety.

  • An officer may also be recognized as a worker if they perform work for someone else.
  • Changes the rules for calculating the income used to set an injured worker's compensation.
  • The CNESST will sometimes have to offer the parties a chance to negotiate after a request for review.
  • Higher fines for breaching the confidentiality of the file of a worker who is a victim of violence, including sexual violence.

  • Sets a maximum time limit for appointing an arbitrator and holding the first day of a grievance hearing.

26675:
• This bill puts in place measures from the 25 March 2025 budget and amends 38 laws or regulations.
  • It affects, among other things, vehicle taxes, child and spousal support, municipal taxation, and Québec pension plan benefits.
  • Act respecting the Québec Pension Plan: work counts as done in Québec only if it is performed in Canada.
  • Act respecting the Québec Pension Plan: the pension calculation removes the months during which a person receives a reduced CNESST benefit for a workplace accident.
  • Highway Safety Code and Regulation respecting road vehicle registration: the value threshold for a vehicle that triggers an additional fee rises from $40,000 to $62,500.
  • Highway Safety Code: electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles lose their tax exemption between $40,000 and $75,000 in value.
  • Highway Safety Code: a new additional fee applies to electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles for registration or road use.
  • Act respecting the Institut de la statistique du Québec: sets out the rules for when the Institute collects information on behalf of a public body.
  • Act respecting the Institut de la statistique du Québec: more researchers linked to public bodies will be able to use information for research purposes.
  • Code of Civil Procedure: changes the formula used to calculate the seizable share of income of a person who owes child or spousal support.
  • Code of Civil Procedure: money received for an adult child under a court order can no longer be seized.
  • Act to facilitate the payment of support: a person receiving social assistance will no longer have to provide a guarantee for the collection of their support payments.
  • Act to facilitate the payment of support: during a state of emergency, the Minister of Finance will be able to set the rules on collection fees and advances paid to support-receiving parents.
  • Tax Administration Act: the calculation of a "large corporation"'s capital will take into account related corporations.
  • Tax Administration Act: tax information can be shared with the Minister of Finance, without the person's consent, to analyze economic policies.
  • Act respecting insurers: life insurers will be able to obtain personal information about a deceased person from Revenu Québec and the Registrar of Civil Status, in order to notify beneficiaries of amounts owed.
  • Act respecting municipal taxation: municipalities will no longer be able to collect a business tax, except for certain fees from business development corporations.
  • Act respecting municipal taxation: municipalities will no longer be able to establish a rental value roll.
  • Budget measure: more money granted to the Fonds Avenir Mécénat Culture.
  • Budget measure: the fee for consulting the land register is revised.
  • Act to reduce the debt: the government's net debt reduction targets are raised for 2032-2033 and 2037-2038.
  • Act respecting parental insurance: the government will be able to change contribution rates for this plan through a government regulation, without a new vote in the National Assembly.

26771:
• This bill merges, abolishes or reorganizes several public bodies to simplify the administration of the state.
  • It also strengthens the accountability rules that apply to senior officials.
Part 1 Act respecting the National Institute of Excellence in Health and Social Services
  • Merges this institute and the National Institute of Public Health into a single body, the Québec Institute of Health and Social Services.
Part 2 Act respecting the governance of the health and social services system
  • Santé Québec's board of directors will also become the board of Urgences-santé.
Part 3 Act respecting Héma-Québec and the Biovigilance Committee
  • Héma-Québec, which manages blood supply, will take over the coordination of organ donations, a task removed from Transplant Québec.
Part 4 Act respecting the Commission d'évaluation de l'enseignement collégial
  • This commission, which evaluated colleges, is abolished.
Part 5 Act establishing the Office Québec-Monde pour la jeunesse
  • This body is folded into the Ministry of International Relations and La Francophonie.
Part 6 Act respecting the Office franco-québécois pour la jeunesse
  • Its internal structure is revised.
Part 7 Act respecting the Centre de la francophonie des Amériques
  • This centre becomes a private non-profit organization instead of a public body.
Part 8 Act respecting parental insurance
  • The Conseil de gestion de l'assurance parentale is abolished; Retraite Québec now manages this plan and its fund.
Part 9 Act respecting the Ministère des Finances
  • The Minister of Finance must present a comprehensive financial plan to fight climate change in the budget.
  • The Québec Cabinet will be able to decide, without a new vote, how to split surpluses from the Electrification and Climate Change Fund between the Generations Fund and the Land Transportation Fund.
Part 10 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale
  • This ministry's Information Technology Fund is abolished, and its money returns to the government's general fund.
  • A similar university fund (Fund 3 for university excellence and performance) is also abolished, with its money transferred to the general fund.
Part 11 Act to combat poverty and social exclusion
  • Two community funds are merged into one, the Fonds québécois d'initiatives sociales et d'action communautaire.
Part 12 Public Service Act
  • The Commission de la fonction publique, which handled complaints from government employees, is abolished; its duties move to the Administrative Labour Tribunal.
  • Public bodies will now be able to provide administrative services to each other, for example Santé Québec providing services to Urgences-santé.
Part 13 Act respecting the marketing of agricultural, food and fish products
  • Reduces the number of vice-presidents and members needed for certain decisions by the Régie des marchés agricoles.
Part 14 Act respecting the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec
  • The Québec Cabinet will now appoint vice-presidents and set their salaries.
Part 15 Act respecting the governance of state-owned enterprises
  • The management of executives at Hydro-Québec, the Commission de la construction du Québec and other state-owned enterprises must be reviewed by a parliamentary committee at least once every four years.
Part 16 Public Administration Act
  • Specifies that every senior official must act with prudence, efficiency and fairness in their duties.
  • A new two-year probationary period will apply to anyone appointed as a senior official.
  • During this probationary period, the Québec Cabinet will be able to dismiss a non-permanent senior official with a simple 15-day written notice.
Part 17 Act respecting contracting by public bodies
  • Businesses will no longer need to periodically renew their authorization to contract with the government.
Part 18 Act respecting the Centre d'acquisitions gouvernementales
  • Its contracts and those carried out for groups of public bodies will follow the same rules as those of government enterprises.
Part 19 Act respecting the Société d'habitation du Québec
  • Allows the Québec Cabinet to merge housing bureaus or create new ones for any chosen territory.
  • Ends the joint management of contributions paid by organizations receiving assistance from the Société d'habitation du Québec.
Part 20 Several financial sector laws
  • Reduce the frequency of certain required reports and remove the obligation to produce certain documents.
Part 21 Act respecting the regulation of the financial sector
  • The Autorité des marchés financiers, which oversees this sector, will have to make certain data and analyses available online.
  • The bill also makes technical adjustments to rules on sustainable development, the chief forester and pay equity.
  • Many other texts and regulations are amended solely to ensure consistency with these changes.

• Changes the way members are elected to the Québec National Assembly.
  • Québec would be divided into 80 ridings and 17 electoral regions.
  • The total number of seats would go from 125 to 129.
  • There would be 80 riding seats and 49 regional seats.
  • Each voter would vote twice: once for a riding candidate, and once for a regional candidate or list.

  • Regional seats would be shared out based on the votes parties receive, to correct gaps between votes and seats.
  • A party would need at least 4% of the votes in Québec to get regional seats.
  • Parties would have to put forward as many women as men on their regional lists.
  • In general elections, riding candidates would have to include 40% to 60% women.
  • Rules on party financing and election spending would be adjusted, without changing the total amount.
  • Rules are set out to replace a member whose regional seat becomes vacant.

26993:
• This bill streamlines the operating rules of professional orders (such as nurses, pharmacists, notaries) and gives more powers to certain health professionals.
  • It also changes the rules around the links between pharmacists, manufacturers and pharmacy chains.
Part 1 Professional Code
  • Professional orders will be able to pass certain regulations without the approval of the Office des professions or the government.
  • The Office des professions, which oversees professional orders, will have to approve codes of ethics instead of the government.
  • The Office will be able to set the diplomas required to obtain a permit, with the government's approval.
  • The Office will have to create a common rule for all orders to settle disputes over professionals' bills.
  • The Office will be able to impose common rules on several orders after consulting them.
  • The Office becomes solely responsible for the ethics rules for members of orders' boards of directors, and will be able to investigate and sanction breaches.
  • The public roll of an order's members will have to include more mandatory information.
  • The minimum number of signatures required to call a special general meeting of an order is changed.
  • Changes are made to the governance rules of certain professional orders.
Part 2 Act respecting nurses
  • Nurses will be able to initiate exams and tests in more situations, not only in public health.
  • They will also be able to prescribe exams, tests, medications, substances, products and dressings according to rules to be set later.
  • The rule requiring only section delegates to vote at general meetings is removed.
Part 3 Midwives Act
  • Midwives will be able to prescribe and provide contraception more easily.
  • They will be able to screen for and treat sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections more broadly, even in a person without symptoms.
Part 4 Optometry Act
  • Optometrists will have fewer restrictions on the medications they can prescribe and the care they can provide.
Part 5 Dietitians-nutritionists
  • Their scope of practice is updated and they will no longer need a medical prescription for certain reserved activities.
Part 6 Psychotherapy
  • The Interdisciplinary Advisory Council on the Practice of Psychotherapy ceases its activities.
  • Marriage and family therapists will be able to practise psychotherapy without a special permit, like psychologists and doctors.
  • The Office will be able to authorize people in training to carry out certain activities reserved for psychotherapists.
  • The Office will be able to create rules to grant a psychotherapist's permit to people already authorized elsewhere in Canada.
Part 7 Act respecting agronomists
  • The definition of the practice of the profession no longer requires that the act be done for payment.
Part 8 Pharmacy Act
  • The government will be able to allow a pharmacist to prescribe or substitute a medication for one made by a company in which they have a financial interest, under specific conditions.
Part 9 Act respecting prescription drug insurance
  • A new rule will allow a drug manufacturer to pay certain benefits to an intermediary, such as a banner or pharmacy chain.
Part 10 Regulation respecting drug manufacturers and wholesalers
  • Manufacturers will also be able to pay these benefits to a drug wholesaler.
  • Several other professional laws (land surveyors, the Barreau, notaries, denturology, medical imaging technologists, legal aid, the Charter of the French Language) receive related consequential adjustments.

  • The government must assess the impact of its decisions on the right to food and mitigate any negative effects.
